questions.q: When is reading a framework's source the right move?
questions.explain: Documentation states promises; source states behaviour. Read it with a precise question, and confirm what you read with an experiment.
options: Before using any function, to be safe
When you need to know exactly what it does in a case the documentation does not settle, like which of two routes wins
Never; the documentation is always enough
Only when the framework has a bug

questions.q: Which question is best for starting to read a framework's source?
questions.explain: A narrow question tells you what to search for and when you are done. Broad questions lead to reading hundreds of files without an answer.

questions.q: A package's exports field lists only ".". What happens to import("@zudojs/http/dist/httpAdapter/httpAdapter.errorResponse.js")?
questions.explain: exports is the package's public boundary. Files outside it may exist on disk, but Node will not load them through the package name.
options: It works, because the file exists
TypeScript compiles it, and it works at runtime

questions.q: The package's files field excludes dist/**/*.map. What does that mean for you when you press "Go to Definition" in your editor?
questions.explain: Without source maps, the declaration is where types lead. Open the neighbouring .js file, or use "Go to Source Definition", to see the code.
options: You land in the original TypeScript source
You land in the .d.ts declaration, because no source maps point back to the TypeScript; the implementation is in the compiled .js files
The editor cannot open the package at all
You land in a minified bundle

questions.q: What can you learn from a package's dependencies before reading any code?
questions.explain: @zudojs/container depends only on errors; @zudojs/http on six packages. Behaviour you see in one may be implemented in a dependency.
options: Which other packages it builds on, and so roughly how large the read is and where some behaviour may come from

questions.q: What is a barrel file?
questions.explain: Reading a barrel first shows which areas a package covers and, through explicit re-exports, how name clashes were resolved.
options: A file with all the tests
An index.js that re-exports other modules, forming the package's table of contents
A file that lists the dependencies

questions.q: compareSegmentSpecificity is exported from @zudojs/http but not mentioned in its documentation. How should you treat it?
questions.explain: Barrels that re-export whole folders make helpers public by accident. Documented API is protected by semantic versioning; incidental exports may change more freely.
options: As exported but incidental: it is reachable, but its authors may not treat it as a stable promise, so depend on it with care
As the main API of the package

questions.q: Why is building on a package's internal module risky, even when you manage to load it?
questions.explain: Semantic versioning protects the public API only. Reading internals to understand behaviour is fine; depending on them turns every upgrade into a risk.
options: Internals can change or disappear in any release, including a patch, without being a breaking change
It is illegal under the MIT license

questions.q: Why read a function's .d.ts declaration before its implementation?
questions.explain: The contract narrows the reading. Knowing that registerFactory types its factory from its inject list tells you what to look for in the code.
options: Declarations are always correct, implementations are not
It is short, it states what the function accepts and returns, and it bounds what the implementation can do

questions.q: What does InjectedDependencies<[Token<Date>, Token<string>]> compute, given { -readonly [K in keyof Deps]: Deps[K] extends ProviderToken<infer U> ? U : never }?
questions.explain: A mapped type over a tuple keeps the positions; infer U extracts each token's type. The result is the factory's parameter list.

questions.q: Why does registerFactory<T, const Deps extends readonly ProviderToken[]> use the const modifier on Deps?
questions.explain: Without it, the list would widen to (Token<Date> | Token<string>)[], and every parameter would have the union type.
options: To make the tokens immutable at runtime
So [CLOCK, SHOP_NAME] is inferred as a tuple, not as an array of a union, and each factory parameter gets its own type
It is required for all generics

questions.q: What is a quick way to see what a complicated type from a .d.ts actually computes?
questions.explain: Types are erased at runtime, so they cannot be printed. The compiler, however, spells out the expected type in its error message, as it did for [Date, string].
options: Assign a value you know is wrong to it and read the compiler's error, which names the expected type

questions.q: You saw the response body {"error":"Internal Server Error"}. What is a good way to find the code that produced it?
questions.explain: Messages and status texts are distinctive and rarely renamed, so they lead straight to the code that uses them. "error" matches everything.
options: Read every file in dist/ from the top
Search dist/ for the exact string "Internal Server Error"

questions.q: The source shows that HttpRouter.match sorts all routes on every call. What is the most sensible reaction?
questions.explain: For a few dozen routes the cost is negligible. A precise report ("sort once when a route is registered") helps everyone; editing node_modules is lost on the next install.
options: Note that it costs O(n log n) per request, judge it against your route count, and report it with a minimal reproduction and a suggested fix
Ignore it; source code does not affect performance

questions.q: In @zudojs/http, /books/:id and /books/:id(\d+) both match /books/42. Which wins?
questions.explain: The ranking compares segment kinds only. A constraint does not change the kind, so registration order decides. Register constrained parameters first.
options: Always the constrained one, because it is more specific
The one registered first, because both are parameters with the same specificity and the tie goes to the lower sequence number

questions.q: A comment in the router says the ranking "used to" be a sum, which let /:p/:q/:r/:s outrank /admin/*rest. Why are such comments valuable to a reader?
questions.explain: History comments are compressed bug reports. The admin bypass is a reminder that route ranking is a security property, not just a convenience.
options: They show the code is old
Each one records an edge case that once broke, which is exactly the kind of case you should test in your own code

questions.q: How does the @zudojs/http adapter decide the status code of a thrown error?
questions.explain: The mapper checks the shape, not the class. Your own error class with statusCode = 410 got a 410, which also lets errors from other libraries carry statuses.
options: Any error with a numeric statusCode from 400 to 599 sets the status (duck typing); everything else is a 500
It parses the message for a number

questions.q: An error with statusCode: 410 and no expose is thrown. What does the client see?
questions.explain: Message and code are included only when the error opts in with expose: true. Details stay private by default, even for 4xx errors from custom classes.

questions.q: You resolve an unregistered class Sms whose constructor is constructor(readonly gateway = "sms.shop.ng"). What does @zudojs/container do?
questions.explain: Auto-registration checks token.length === 0, and Function.prototype.length stops counting at the first parameter with a default. That is convenient, and surprising if you expected an error.
options: Registers it automatically as transient and builds it with the default gateway, because its length is 0

questions.q: Why does @zudojs/container pass a singletonAncestor down the resolution instead of scanning the path?
questions.explain: Carrying the answer down avoids re-scanning the path at every step, and makes the rule explicit: once a singleton is above you, nothing scoped may be built.
options: It knows the nearest singleton above the current token in O(1), so a scoped token reached below any singleton, even through transients, is detected as captive
To allow singletons to hold scoped objects

questions.q: When you run npx tsc, how does npm find the program to run?
questions.explain: bin maps command names to files. npx uses the local install when there is one, and the #!/usr/bin/env node line makes the file executable as a Node script.
options: It downloads the latest TypeScript every time
It looks up tsc in the bin fields of installed packages and runs that file, whose shebang line says to use Node
It searches your source code for a tsc function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: length counts parameters before the first one with a default value, and never counts rest parameters. A container that auto-registers classes with length === 0 therefore treats Sms as parameterless.

questions.q: This is the comparison rule read from the router (literal 3, parameter 2, wildcard 1, compared left to right). What does this print?
questions.explain: All three literal-first routes beat the catch-all at the first segment. Among them, new (3) beats :id (2), which beats *rest (1), at the second segment. Length never enters into it, which is what fixed the admin bypass.

questions.q: Here is the old rule the comment describes: sum the segment scores. What does this print?
questions.explain: Four parameters sum to 8, beating 3 + 1. With a sum, a long generic route could steal requests from a guarded prefix; comparing left to right makes the literal admin decide first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With equal specificity, the sequence decides. Registered second, the constrained route never gets a chance; registered first, it takes the digits and lets b1 fall through.

questions.q: This mirrors the router's normalizeResponse. What does this print?
questions.explain: Plain data becomes a 200 JSON response, nothing becomes 204 No Content, and a real response object is passed through with its own status. That is why a handler can simply return a book.

questions.q: This mirrors the adapter's error mapper. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only 4xx and 5xx statuses count, so a 302 on an error is ignored and becomes a 500. The message goes out only with expose: true.
options:
410 (status text)
410 Book b7 is out of print
500 Internal Server Error
500 Internal Server Error

410 Book b7 is out of print
410 Book b7 is out of print
302 (status text)
500 Internal Server Error

410 (status text)
410 Book b7 is out of print
302 (status text)
500 Internal Server Error

500 Internal Server Error
410 Book b7 is out of print
500 Internal Server Error
500 Internal Server Error

questions.q: This resolves a subpath against an exports map the way Node does for exact keys. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only listed subpaths are reachable. A package can publish a second entry point such as ./testing on purpose; everything else stays internal even though the file is in the tarball.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An object maps command names to files; a string means one command named after the package (without its scope). A library such as @zudojs/http has no bin at all.

questions.q: Write definedIn(files, name): return the paths of files that contain export function <name>( or export class <name> followed by a space or {. The program should print [ 'dist/router/factory.js' ] and [ 'dist/router/register.js' ].
questions.explain: Searching for the definition pattern, not the bare name, skips imports, comments and similarly named classes such as HttpRouterGroup. The space or brace after the class name is what excludes it.

questions.q: Write excerpt(text, from, count): find the first line matching the regular expression from, and return count lines from there, each prefixed with its 1-based line number padded with zeros to 3 digits and two spaces. The program should print the three lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Quoting with line numbers from the installed file makes a reading checkable: anyone can open the same file at the same line, and a later version that moves the code will visibly change the excerpt.

questions.q: Write reexports(text) that lists the module paths of every export * from "…" line in a barrel, and explicit(text) that lists the names from export { a, b } from "…" lines. The program should print the two lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: The star exports are the package's areas; the explicit ones are the names whose ownership had to be decided. Both come from reading one file, before any implementation.

questions.q: Write resolve(token, singletonAncestor?) for this registry. It throws captive: <ancestor> -> <token> when a scoped token is reached with a singleton above it, passes the nearest singleton down to dependencies, and returns the token name otherwise. The program should print the three lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Resolved on their own, Checkout and Formatter may use the scoped cart. Below Report, a singleton, the same Formatter would capture it, and the ancestor carried down detects that without scanning the path.
questions.expected:
Checkout: Checkout
Formatter: Formatter
Report: captive: Report -> Cart

questions.q: Write canAutoRegister(ctor) using the rule read from the container (ctor.length === 0), and print for each class whether it can be auto-registered. Then explain to yourself why Sms surprises. The program should print Clock true, Mailer false, Sms true.
questions.explain: A parameter with a default does not count in length, so Sms looks parameterless and is built with its default. Knowing the exact rule turns a surprise into a decision: register Sms explicitly if the gateway must come from configuration.
questions.expected:
Clock true
Mailer false
Sms true

questions.q: Two routers with the same routes answer three requests. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both give the same answer; one sorts on every request, the other once. That is the whole content of the improvement you would suggest after reading HttpRouter.match: same behaviour, less work per request.

questions.q: This mirrors the container's cycle check, with a path array and a Set. What does this print?
questions.explain: The path starts where the resolution started, so the chain names the cycle from Payments. finally removes each token when its branch ends, so siblings that share a dependency are not mistaken for a cycle.
options:
Clock
circular: Payments -> Invoices -> Orders -> Payments

Clock
circular: Orders -> Payments -> Invoices -> Orders

circular: Clock
circular: Payments -> Invoices -> Orders -> Payments

questions.q: Rewrite Router so it sorts its routes once in add instead of in every match, keeping the same answers (literal segments before parameters, ties by registration order). The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Sorting happens once per registration, at startup, instead of once per request, forever: three routes, three sorts, however many requests arrive. The answers are unchanged because the comparison and the tie-break (the sequence number) are the same.

questions.q: Write findStatus(error) like the adapter's mapper: if the error has a numeric statusCode from 400 to 599, return it; if it is a PipelineError wrapper, look at its cause (at most 8 levels deep); otherwise return 500. The program should print 404 404 500 502.
questions.explain: Only the framework's own wrapper is looked through. An application error that merely has a cause ends the search (500), so a cause attached for logging is never exposed, and a deliberate 502 is not replaced by the upstream's 401. The depth limit protects against cyclic causes.
